title: I’ll Say it... GLP1’s are a Longevity Drug and they Work Better in Women than Men
description: Team, I was on FaceTime with my sister-in-law yesterday. She’s 47, she’s been trying for months to get back to the strongest version of herself, and she’s doing everything right, or everything she’s been told is right, and it isn’t quite working. So I mentioned GLP-1s. Gently. Just as one thing worth understanding. And her face changed. “Aren’t those the ones that make your hair fall out and eat your muscle?” She’d read the posts. The muscle loss, the thinning hair, the gaunt “Ozempic face.” She was scared of them, and she couldn’t actually tell me what they did or how they worked. She just knew she was supposed to be afraid. And I sat there thinking, this is one of the most-studied drugs in modern medicine, and one of the smartest women I know is terrified of it based on captions. That conversation is why I’m writing to you today. Because my sister-in-law is not unusual. She’s the rule. Most people I talk to are frightened of these drugs and fascinated by them at the same time, and almost nobody has been given the honest version. So let me give it to you. Because two days ago, something landed that changes the conversation entirely. A team at UC Berkeley took a group of old female mice, the mouse equivalent of a woman in her late 60s, and gave half of them a GLP-1 drug. The same class of drug as Ozempic and Wegovy. Not from youth. From old age. And the mice that got the drug lived meaningfully longer than the ones that didn’t. Their median lifespan went from 742 days to 834 days. That’s about 12% more life, and it was published in Nature two days ago (Feng et al., 2026). From Feng et al., Nature (2026), used under CC BY 4.0.

title: What Is Brain Span? The Midlife Window That Decides Alzheimer’s Risk in Women
description: Team, Lifespan is how long you live. Healthspan is how long you stay well. Brain span is how long your mind still works: memory, judgment, language, the ability to stay yourself. That is the number I care about as a clinical neurophysiologist. And it is not a 70-year-old number. Alzheimer’s pathology can start between 45 and 65, years to decades before anyone forgets a name. Average age at diagnosis is 72. By then the window where you could have changed the trajectory has been open, and mostly ignored, for twenty years. For women, that window has a name. It is midlife. It is the menopause transition. Lisa Mosconi’s March 2026 review in the Journal of Clinical Investigation calls it what it is: the front line of Alzheimer prevention . Nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer’s are women. A 45-year-old woman’s lifetime risk is about 1 in 5, twice that of a man the same age. Longevity does not fully explain that gap!! Alzheimer’s is a midlife disease that shows up late We keep treating Alzheimer’s as a disease of old age because that is when we diagnose it. The plaques, the tangles, the drop in the brain’s glucose metabolism: those are already moving in the years around menopause. Mosconi’s imaging synthesis is blunt. Postmenopausal women, and to a lesser extent perimenopausal women, carry a heavier Alzheimer’s biomarker load than premenopausal women and than men of the same age: more amyloid, more tau, lower brain glucose use, less gray matter in the regions Alzheimer’s hits first. Those differences survived age adjustment. Mosconi still flags that postmenopausal women are typically older, so residual aging cannot be ruled out. Endocrine change is the leading explanation, not a closed case.

title: Jim Kwik: Your Brain Has a Savings Account. You're Probably Draining It.
description: Team, Jim Kwik was called “the boy with the broken brain” by a teacher, out loud, when he was nine. A brain injury at five left him years behind. He’s now the brain coach Hollywood actors and CEOs hire to think faster. So when he talks about what a brain can rebuild, I listen. We met to talk about AI. But the thing I keep coming back to is simpler, and it’s the most useful way to think about your brain I’ve heard in a long time. He calls cognitive reserve a savings account. It’s real neuroscience, and it’s why two people can have the same Alzheimer’s pathology in their brains while one loses their memory and the other stays sharp at 90. The reserve is the buffer. You spend a lifetime building the balance, and it’s what protects you when things start to go wrong underneath. Every day, you either make a deposit or take a withdrawal. The withdrawals are the ones you already suspect: bad sleep, chronic stress, sitting all day, processed food. But Jim named a new one. Every time you let a machine do your thinking, that’s a withdrawal. He pointed to an MIT study where people wrote essays with ChatGPT, with Google, or with just their heads. The AI group had the least brain engagement and barely remembered what they’d written. His line: you don’t go to the gym and have someone lift the weights for you. But that’s what we’re doing with our minds all day. The deposits are small, free, and completely in your hands. This is the part your evening is made of: Read the actual book, not the AI summary. Do the tip math in your head. Kill the calculator for small stuff. Sit in a boring moment instead of grabbing your phone.
